title: Nessa and the Silent Kites
markdown:
Gold spilled over the jagged peaks. Dawn was sharp, and for Nessa the ridge courier, whose eyes were the colour of a storm-cleared sky, the wind had lost its cheerful whistle. It sounded like a hush pretending to be weather.

Pol the weather vane maker tugged at his windswept hair. He noticed what other people called nothing.

“Nessa. The kites. They’re not flying right.”

Kites were the sky-language of the lookout posts, each pattern a sentence of peace. Pol’s custom vanes, perched atop each post, usually spun with bright abandon. Today they hung limp.

“Bribed?” Nessa said, and the word sat in her stomach like a stone. The Grayscale Clan traded loyalty for coin. Their shadows were longer this morning.

“The path to the northern lookout is clear,” Pol said, sketching on a dusty slate. “Beyond that, the eastern ridge. Lightning-struck. No one goes there.”

“No one usually goes there,” Nessa said. The lowlands slept. The Clan would not stop at silencing lookouts; scouts were already creeping closer. She could almost taste metal on the crisp air. “We have to warn them.”

They pushed through dew-kissed scrub, boots crunching on pebbles with a determined rhythm. The air, cool and charged, whispered urgency. Each step took them higher toward the jagged teeth of the eastern ridge. The usual comforting bird song was absent, replaced by an eerie hush. Then a rumble, deep, guttural, not thunder. It vibrated through their boots.

“The Grayscale scouts,” Pol gasped, pointing. His keen eyes were wide. “They’ve already crossed the lower pass. They’re moving fast.”

Panic threatened. Nessa grabbed his arm, grip strong. “Not here. Not now.” Her voice, though tight, held determination. “We move. Fast. Stick to the shadows. Use the twists. Don’t give them a clear shot.”

They scrambled up the slick dark rock, movements quick and precise. Lightning-scarred trees clawed at the sky like skeletal fingers. The wind howled, a tempest unleashed. A sudden crack sent them diving behind a massive boulder. A shadowy figure, cloaked and silent, darted past, eyes like chips of obsidian.

“Too close,” Nessa puffed, heart hammering, breath in short sharp bursts. “Pol, the detour. Is there another way?”

He scanned the drop. “A narrow ledge. It bypasses the main path. The wind whips the corners.”

“We take it.”

The ledge was barely a handspan wide, a precarious ribbon of stone. The wind shrieked, threatening to tear them from their hold. Nessa moved first, her courier’s instinct guiding sure feet. Pol followed, keen observation finding the faintest handholds.

A guttural roar echoed from above. A Grayscale warrior, larger and more menacing, appeared on the path they had just left, a cruel smirk stretching his scarred face. He brandished a heavy spiked club. He was cutting them off.

“He’s blocking the way back,” Pol yelled. “He’ll wait for us.”

Nessa looked at the sheer drop, then at the angry warrior. Inspiration glinted. “Pol. Your strongest cord. The one for the big vanes.”

Pol fumbled in his pack and thrust the thick sturdy cord into her hand. Nessa snatched it, mind racing. With a burst of adrenaline she tied one end securely to a jagged rock.

“When I say go, you pull with all your might. Then you run. Don’t look back.”

She waited, gaze fixed. The warrior took a step, club raised. “Go.”

Pol yanked with everything he had. The cord, taut as a bowstring, whipped out and tangled the warrior’s ankles. He roared in surprise as he lost his footing, tumbling down the rocky slope, club clattering away.

They did not wait for wonder. They scrambled, breath catching, the roar of wind and distant shouts fading. They burst through a tangle of thorny bushes and tumbled into a clearing. Below, bathed in the soft golden glow of the rising sun, lay the lowlands: cottages dotted the landscape, smoke curling lazily from chimneys, a place that did not yet know it had been nearly spoken for.

They burst into the village square, a whirlwind of dust.

“Attack,” Nessa gasped, voice raw. “The Grayscale Clan. The lookouts are silent.”

A gasp among the early risers. Fear, then the slower thing: belief. Pol stood beside her, streaked with grime.

“We warned you,” he said.

They looked toward the darkening horizon. The kites still hung lifeless on the posts above, but the vanes in the square, at least, had begun to twitch, as if the morning were trying, cautiously, to remember how to move.
characters: Nessa (a ridge courier), Pol (the weather vane maker)
